stem: A 64-year-old woman has had headaches for 25 years and takes several tablets of one of her medications every day. She now has flank pain and passes blood in her urine. Blood pressure is 158/96 mm Hg, creatinine is 2.4 mg/dL, and urinalysis shows sterile pyuria. CT shows small kidneys with sloughed tissue in the renal pelvis. She also takes digoxin, nifedipine, propranolol and warfarin.
oneliner: 64F + 25 y headaches + several tablets of one drug daily + hematuria, flank pain + Cr 2.4 + sterile pyuria + small kidneys with sloughed papillae + also digoxin, nifedipine, propranolol, warfarin → which drug?
ask: Which drug most likely caused her kidney disease?

whyNot.A: **Cardiac glycoside**: toxicity gives arrhythmias and visual changes, not papillary necrosis
whyNot.B: **Dihydropyridine**: causes edema and flushing, not kidney damage
whyNot.C: **Beta-blocker**: bradycardia and bronchospasm, not kidney damage
whyNot.D: **Anticoagulant**: bleeding is the danger; does not cause papillary necrosis

why: **Years of high daily analgesic use + sterile pyuria + small kidneys + sloughed papillae** = analgesic nephropathy with papillary necrosis, caused by chronic **aspirin / NSAID** use.

drug.name: Aspirin (NSAIDs)
drug.how: Irreversibly acetylates COX-1 and COX-2, lowering prostaglandins and thromboxane
drug.use: Analgesia, antipyresis, antiplatelet therapy, Kawasaki disease
drug.watch: Gastric ulcers, tinnitus, analgesic nephropathy and papillary necrosis, Reye syndrome in children, respiratory alkalosis then anion gap acidosis in overdose

stem: A 68-year-old man with heart failure and reduced ejection fraction takes lisinopril and furosemide. His cardiologist adds spironolactone. Two weeks later he feels weak, and his creatinine has crept up. The ECG shows tall, narrow, peaked T waves.
oneliner: 68M + HFrEF on lisinopril, furosemide + spironolactone added 2 wk ago + weakness, creatinine up + peaked T waves → which electrolyte problem?
ask: Which of the following electrolyte disturbances most likely developed?

whyNot.A: Aldosterone blockade **retains** potassium; low K+ would flatten T waves and add U waves
whyNot.C: Low sodium does not **peak the T waves**; that ECG change points to potassium
whyNot.D: Aldosterone blockade gives a **mild acidosis** (less H+ secretion), the opposite of alkalosis
whyNot.E: Not linked to these drugs, and it would **shorten the QT**, not peak the T waves

why: **Peaked T waves** with weakness point to high potassium. **Spironolactone blocks aldosterone** in the collecting duct so K+ is not secreted, and the **ACE inhibitor lowers aldosterone** further; falling renal function adds to the load.

drug.name: Spironolactone
drug.how: Blocks mineralocorticoid receptors in the collecting duct, so less Na+ is reabsorbed and less K+ and H+ are secreted
drug.use: HFrEF (mortality benefit), resistant hypertension, primary hyperaldosteronism, ascites, hirsutism
drug.watch: Hyperkalemia (worse with ACE inhibitor, ARB, CKD), gynecomastia, antiandrogen effects

idea.rule: Anything that lowers aldosterone action or blocks distal K+ secretion can cause hyperkalemia.
